definition: NOx is the generic term for nitrogen oxide (NO) and nitrogen dioxide (NO2), formed when high combustion temperatures force atmospheric nitrogen (78% of air) to react with oxygen supplied by the combustion air.
core_idea: Because combustion draws its oxygen from air that is mostly nitrogen, sufficiently hot flames inevitably create some NOx; in sunlight this breaks down and contributes to ground-level ozone (smog) and acid rain, both of which have direct respiratory health impacts.
key_points: Nitrogen is inert, colorless, and odorless under normal conditions but reacts with oxygen at high combustion temperatures.
NOx is a generic label covering both NO and NO2.
Sunlight breaks apart NOx molecules, generating ozone (O3).
Ozone/smog causes shortness of breath, chest pain, asthma, and coughing attacks.
NOx also contributes to acid rain formation.
NOx pollution is typically managed as a localized/regional issue rather than a global one.
relationships: NO2, a form of NOx, acts as the catalyst that converts SO2 into sulfuric acid (see SOx item).
trading_implications: Regional rather than global NOx regulation implies compliance costs and any emissions-trading exposure are geography-specific for generators, distinct from global CO2 regimes.
caveats: It's easy to assume NOx comes mainly from nitrogen contained in the fuel itself; the text attributes it primarily to atmospheric nitrogen reacting at high combustion temperature.
